1. Introduction & Spectrum of Marine Injury

Tintinalli Ch.213 p.1363
  • Marine injuries fall into three broad categories: traumatic injuries from animal contact, envenomations from specialized stinging/venom apparatus, and contact dermatitis.
  • Most fatalities are from large predator attacks (sharks, crocodiles, alligators) — but most ED visits are from minor wounds, jellyfish stings, and sea urchin spines.
  • Marine wound infection patterns are distinct from terrestrial — high prevalence of Vibrio, Aeromonas, and Mycobacterium marinum.
  • Many envenomations respond to hot-water immersion because most marine venoms are heat-labile proteins.

2. Major Marine Trauma

Tintinalli p.1363

Common attackers

  • Sharks — bite force can cause severe avulsion and exsanguination; major causes of mortality are hemorrhage and drowning.
  • Barracuda, moray eels, groupers, sea lions — penetrating bites; secondary infection common.
  • Crocodiles, alligators — crush + tear; high contamination; require aggressive irrigation, antibiotics, surgical exploration.

Initial management — bleeding control

  1. Direct pressure / pressure dressings; consider arterial tourniquets if extremity hemorrhage uncontrolled.
  2. Fluid resuscitation with crystalloid (and blood products if hemorrhagic shock).
  3. Tetanus prophylaxis per immunization status.
  4. Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics covering marine organisms (see Section 4).
  5. Imaging: radiographs for retained foreign bodies (teeth, spines, hooks); CT for deep injury.
  6. Surgical consultation for vascular injury, deep wounds, or suspected nerve/tendon damage.
⚠️ Pearl — Shark bite hemorrhage: primary cause of death in shark attack is hemorrhage, often from femoral or brachial artery. Tourniquet placement on land + rapid transport saves lives.

3. Minor Marine Wounds & Bacteriology

Tintinalli p.1363–1364

Coral abrasions and minor wounds

  • Most marine stings and minor injuries do not cause severe injury but have a high secondary infection rate.
  • Wounds typically resolve in 1–2 weeks but may take up to 6 weeks if infection develops.
  • Vinegar (5% acetic acid) can be used for some envenomations (jellyfish, fireworms — see species-specific sections); not for general lacerations.
📚 Fig 213-1 — Coral wound from a swimmer thrown against a reef; coral wounds frequently retain debris (Tintinalli p.1364)

Marine pathogens (bacteriology)

  • Polymicrobial: streptococci, staphylococci, and gram-negatives are common; the marine environment adds:
  • Vibrio vulnificus, V. parahaemolyticus, V. alginolyticus — saltwater; particularly virulent in cirrhotic, immunocompromised, and diabetic patients (sepsis, hemorrhagic bullae, mortality 30–50%).
  • Aeromonas hydrophila — freshwater (also brackish); cellulitis to NSTI.
  • Mycobacterium marinum — "fish tank granuloma"; chronic, indolent.
  • Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae — fish handlers; localized cellulitis.
  • Edwardsiella, Streptococcus iniae, Pseudomonas, Chromobacterium.
Pearl — Vibrio in cirrhotic patients: raw oyster ingestion or saltwater wound + cirrhosis = high risk for fulminant V. vulnificus sepsis with hemorrhagic bullae. Treat empirically with doxycycline + ceftriaxone (or fluoroquinolone). Mortality up to 50% even with treatment.

Wound management

  • Aggressive irrigation with saline.
  • Remove foreign bodies (coral, spines, teeth) — meticulous debridement.
  • Do NOT suture heavily contaminated puncture wounds or marine envenomation wounds — leave open or delayed primary closure.
  • Tetanus prophylaxis.
  • Antibiotics — see Tables 213-1, 213-2.

4. Antibiotic Selection for Marine Wounds

Tintinalli Tables 213-1, 213-2 p.1363
📚 Table 213-1 — Recommendations for Antibiotic Treatment of Marine-Associated Wounds (Tintinalli p.1363)
📚 Table 213-2 — Antibiotics for Marine-Associated Wound Infections by Water Type (Tintinalli p.1363)

Empiric choices by water type

WaterLikely organismsEmpiric coverage
Salt waterVibrio species, plus skin floraDoxycycline + ceftriaxone (or third-gen cephalosporin)
Fresh waterAeromonas + skin floraFluoroquinolone (or TMP-SMX) + first-gen cephalosporin
All marine wounds (skin/strep cover)Staph + strepFirst-gen cephalosporin or anti-staph penicillin

Indications for prophylactic antibiotics

  • Deep puncture wounds, retained foreign body, devitalized tissue.
  • Wounds in immunocompromised (cirrhosis, DM, HIV, chemo, asplenia) → broaden coverage to include Vibrio.
  • Wounds with significant inflammation or systemic features.
  • Coral or stingray puncture wounds with envenomation.
Inline MCQ 1. A 60-year-old cirrhotic patient develops fever, hemorrhagic bullae, and shock 24 h after stepping on a sharp shell while swimming in salt water. Empiric antibiotic regimen?
A. Cephalexin PO
B. Vancomycin alone
C. Doxycycline + ceftriaxone (covers Vibrio)
D. TMP-SMX alone
Answer: C. Cirrhotic + saltwater + hemorrhagic bullae + sepsis = V. vulnificus. Doxycycline + 3rd-gen cephalosporin is standard. Mortality ~50%. Reference: Tintinalli p.1363.

5. Stingray & Venomous Fish (Catfish, Lionfish, Stonefish, Weeverfish)

Tintinalli p.1364

Stingrays

  • Tail spine inflicts laceration, often retains a piece of integumentary sheath that releases venom.
  • Most stings on the lower extremity (stepping on rays in shallow water — "shuffle" precaution).
  • Pain peaks within 30–90 min; can radiate up the limb.
  • Severe stings to chest/abdomen can be fatal (cardiac penetration).

Venomous fish (Scorpaenidae family)

  • Stonefish (Synanceia) — most venomous fish; severe envenomation can be life-threatening. Indo-Pacific.
  • Lionfish, scorpionfish — common saltwater aquarium pets; envenomation similar but milder than stonefish.
  • Weeverfish (Trachinus) — Mediterranean and European waters, sandy bottom dwellers.
  • Catfish — freshwater and saltwater; spines on dorsal and pectoral fins.

Clinical features

  • Immediate intense local pain — often severe and disproportionate.
  • Swelling, erythema, possible necrosis.
  • Systemic symptoms: nausea, vomiting, weakness, syncope, dysrhythmia (severe stonefish).

Treatment

  1. Hot-water immersion 110°F (43°C) to 114°F (45.6°C) for 30–90 min — denatures heat-labile venom proteins. First-line for ALL marine envenomations.
  2. Wound exploration and debridement — remove visible spine fragments; image (radiograph or US) for retained foreign body if pain doesn't resolve.
  3. Local anesthetic infiltration (lidocaine without epinephrine) for severe pain; regional nerve block.
  4. Tetanus prophylaxis.
  5. Antibiotic prophylaxis for puncture wounds: doxycycline + ceftriaxone (saltwater) or fluoroquinolone (freshwater).
  6. Stonefish antivenom (CSL Limited, Australia) — for severe systemic envenomation; pretreat with antihistamines (equine source).
Hot-water immersion pearl: 110–114°F (43–46°C) for 30–90 min. Test water on uninjured limb first to avoid scald injury. Continue for 30 min after pain relief or until 90 min total. Most marine venoms denature with heat.
Inline MCQ 2. First-line treatment for a stingray envenomation with severe local pain is:
A. Cold compress
B. Hot-water immersion 110–114°F (43–46°C) for 30–90 min
C. Antivenom
D. Steroids
Answer: B. Hot-water immersion denatures heat-labile venom proteins; first-line for stingrays, scorpaenids, sea urchins, etc. Reference: Tintinalli p.1364.

6. Sea Snake

Tintinalli p.1364
  • Family Hydrophiidae — mostly Indo-Pacific waters (also Indian Ocean coastal Asia).
  • Not found in Atlantic, Caribbean, or North American coastal waters.
  • Approximately 50 species; the most dangerous is Enhydrina schistosa, which has caused fatalities in SE Asia.
  • Highly potent neurotoxic + myotoxic venom — among most toxic snake venoms (10–40× more toxic than terrestrial cobra venom).
  • Bite is often painless; envenomation occurs in only ~25% of bites.

Clinical features

  • Local: minimal pain; small puncture marks; no significant local reaction.
  • Systemic (delayed onset 30 min – 8 h):
    • Generalized malaise, anxiety
    • Muscle pain, stiffness
    • Trismus, ptosis, dysphagia
    • Ascending flaccid paralysis (similar to elapid bite)
    • Rhabdomyolysis — myoglobinuria, hyperkalemia → AKI
    • Respiratory failure if severe

Treatment

  • Pressure-immobilization bandage over entire limb (similar to elapid first aid) — slows venom dissemination.
  • Polyvalent sea snake antivenom (CSL Australia) — cross-reactive with most species.
  • Supportive ventilation if respiratory paralysis.
  • Aggressive crystalloid + monitoring for rhabdomyolysis-induced AKI.
  • Observe ≥8 h for any neuro/myo features even if asymptomatic at presentation.

7. Octopus & Cone Snail

Tintinalli p.1365

Blue-ringed octopus (Hapalochlaena)

  • Indo-Pacific; small but extremely venomous.
  • Bite is small, often painless puncture; numbness develops within minutes.
  • Venom = tetrodotoxin — sodium channel blocker → flaccid paralysis and respiratory failure.
  • Onset of paralysis: minutes to 3 hours; recovery typically within 4–10 hours.
  • No antivenom available.
  • Treatment: pressure immobilization + supportive ventilation — patients can survive with prolonged mechanical ventilation until venom effects wear off.

Cone snails (Conus)

  • Tropical reefs; attractive shells lead to handling.
  • Venom delivered via radular dart (fine, hollow tooth-like structure).
  • Venom = mixture of conotoxins (sodium and calcium channel blockers).
  • Local pain + numbness → ascending paralysis → respiratory failure.
  • Mortality 65% for severe C. geographus envenomation.
  • No antivenom; pressure-immobilization + supportive care.
📚 Fig 213-2 — Octopus bite — A) initial scab; B) chronic non-healing ulcer (Tintinalli p.1366)
⚠️ Tetrodotoxin pearl: blue-ringed octopus, pufferfish (Fugu), and certain newts contain tetrodotoxin — a Na+ channel blocker causing rapidly progressive flaccid paralysis. No antidote. Survival depends on prompt pressure-immobilization and intubation/ventilation until venom wears off (typically 4–10 hours).

8. Sea Urchin & Starfish

Tintinalli p.1366 + Table 213-3
📚 Table 213-3 — Early Treatment of Marine Envenomations by Organism (Tintinalli p.1365)

Sea urchin

  • Stepping on or contacting urchin → spines penetrate skin; multiple entry points.
  • Spines may break and remain embedded — chronic granuloma if not removed.
  • Some species (especially with venomous pedicellariae like Toxopneustes) cause systemic envenomation.
  • Sharp spines (most common) — local pain, edema, retained foreign bodies.
📚 Fig 213-3 — Sea urchin sting with multiple entry points (Tintinalli p.1366)

Starfish

  • Crown-of-thorns starfish (Acanthaster planci) — Indo-Pacific reef; long sharp spines deliver mucus venom.
  • Severe burning pain, edema, systemic symptoms (nausea, vomiting, paralysis rare).

Treatment

  1. Hot-water immersion 110–114°F for 30–90 min — relieves pain.
  2. Remove visible spines with forceps. Use US/radiograph for retained fragments.
  3. Surgical removal for retained joint or deep spines.
  4. Topical antibiotics for superficial wounds; systemic antibiotics if signs of infection.
  5. Tetanus prophylaxis.
  6. Outpatient orthopedic follow-up if joint involvement.

9. Jellyfish (Cnidaria) — General

Tintinalli p.1366–1367

Mechanism — Nematocysts

  • Jellyfish tentacles contain millions of nematocysts — microscopic capsules with coiled barbed threads that fire on contact.
  • Each nematocyst delivers a small dose of venom; thousands fire from each contact.
  • Tentacles can continue to discharge nematocysts even when severed from the animal.

Portuguese man-of-war (Physalia physalis)

  • Atlantic, Mediterranean, Pacific, Australian waters.
  • Float-and-tentacle structure (not a true jellyfish — colonial siphonophore).
  • Tentacles up to 30+ meters long.
  • Severe pain at contact; whip-like erythematous lines following tentacle pattern.
  • Systemic effects: nausea, vomiting, weakness, dyspnea, hypotension; rare deaths.
📚 Fig 213-4 — Portuguese man-of-war (Physalia) with characteristic blue float and trailing tentacles (Tintinalli p.1367)

General Cnidarian sting treatment

  1. Remove patient from water — do NOT rub area.
  2. Inactivate nematocysts — depends on species (see below).
  3. Remove visible tentacles with forceps or gloved hand; do not touch with bare skin.
  4. Hot-water immersion 113°F (45°C) for 20 min — preferred for pain relief in Australian box jellyfish, Portuguese man-of-war, and most Cnidarians.
  5. Topical lidocaine for pain; topical steroid for itching.
  6. Systemic analgesics, antihistamines, steroids for severe reactions.

Nematocyst inactivation

OrganismEffectiveAVOID
Box jellyfish (Chironex)Vinegar (5% acetic acid)Fresh water (triggers firing)
Portuguese man-of-warHot water; salt water rinseVinegar (controversial — may trigger firing in some species)
Other jellyfishSalt water rinse + hot-water immersionFresh water; rubbing
AllSalt-water rinseFresh water; alcohol; urine (myth — does not help and may worsen)

10. Box Jellyfish & Irukandji Syndrome

Tintinalli p.1367

Box jellyfish (Chironex fleckeri)

  • Indo-Pacific (especially northern Australia, Philippines, Japan, US Gulf).
  • Most venomous marine animal in the world.
  • Cardiotoxic + neurotoxic + dermatonecrotic venom.
  • Severe envenomation can kill within minutes.
  • Cardiotoxicity can cause cardiac arrest before patient reaches hospital.

Clinical presentation

  • Immediate excruciating pain at contact site.
  • Whip-like ladder/cross-hatch pattern — follows tentacle imprint.
  • Cardiac arrhythmia, hypertension, hypotension, cardiac arrest.
  • Skin necrosis, scarring.
📚 Fig 213-5 — Box jellyfish sting with characteristic ladder/cross-hatch pattern (Tintinalli p.1367)

Treatment

  1. Remove from water; CPR if cardiac arrest.
  2. Vinegar (5% acetic acid) immediately to the affected area for 30 seconds — inactivates nematocysts of Chironex.
  3. Pressure-immobilization NOT recommended — may cause more nematocysts to fire.
  4. Box jellyfish antivenom (CSL Australia) — for severe envenomation, cardiac arrest, or large stings (3–6 vials IV).
  5. Aggressive supportive care: pressors, ACLS, antiarrhythmics.
  6. Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV — adjunct for cardiac dysrhythmias and severe envenomation.

Irukandji syndrome (Carukia barnesi)

  • Northern Australian waters.
  • Sting initially mild → 30 min later: severe systemic effects.
  • Severe HTN, tachycardia, "feeling of impending doom," vomiting, diaphoresis, cramping.
  • Hypertension can be severe enough to cause hemorrhagic stroke or pulmonary edema.
  • Magnesium sulfate 10 mg/kg IV — controls HTN and reduces catecholamine surge.
  • Opioids for severe pain.
  • Phentolamine for refractory HTN.
  • Supportive care; hospitalize 24 h.
⚠️ Pearl — Box jellyfish vinegar: 5% acetic acid (household vinegar) inactivates Chironex nematocysts. Do NOT use fresh water or rub the area — these trigger more nematocyst firing. Antivenom is life-saving in severe cases.
Inline MCQ 3. The most appropriate immediate treatment for a confirmed box jellyfish (Chironex) sting is:
A. Fresh water rinse
B. Vinegar (5% acetic acid) for 30 seconds, then antivenom for severe cases
C. Pressure-immobilization bandage
D. Ice packs
Answer: B. Vinegar inactivates Chironex nematocysts. Pressure-immobilization is contraindicated for box jellyfish (causes nematocyst firing). Reference: Tintinalli p.1367.
Inline MCQ 4. A patient swimming in northern Australia develops mild local sting → 30 minutes later: severe HTN (200/120), tachycardia, "impending doom" sensation, severe back pain. The likely diagnosis is:
A. Stingray envenomation
B. Stonefish envenomation
C. Irukandji syndrome (Carukia barnesi)
D. Sea snake bite
Answer: C. Mild initial sting → delayed catecholamine storm + HTN + impending doom — classic Irukandji. Treat with magnesium sulfate. Reference: Tintinalli p.1367.
Inline MCQ 5. The most useful adjunct medication for severe Irukandji syndrome is:
A. Albuterol
B. Atropine
C. Magnesium sulfate IV
D. Naloxone
Answer: C. Magnesium sulfate 10 mg/kg IV — controls catecholamine surge and HTN in Irukandji. Reference: Tintinalli p.1367.
Inline MCQ 6. The blue-ringed octopus delivers which neurotoxin?
A. α-latrotoxin
B. Tetrodotoxin (Na⁺ channel blocker)
C. Acetylcholinesterase
D. Conotoxin
Answer: B. Tetrodotoxin causes Na+ channel blockade → flaccid paralysis. NO antidote — supportive ventilation until venom wears off. Reference: Tintinalli p.1365.

11. Disposition

Tintinalli p.1367
  • Discharge home after wound care if asymptomatic and no envenomation: ~75% of marine wounds.
  • Admit/observe: significant envenomation (stingray with systemic signs, jellyfish severe reactions, Irukandji ≥24 h, suspected Vibrio in cirrhotic).
  • ICU: box jellyfish severe envenomation, sea snake with neurotoxicity, blue-ringed octopus / cone snail awaiting recovery from paralysis, severe shark bite trauma.
  • Counseling:
    • Watch for delayed signs of envenomation 24 h.
    • Wound check at 24–48 h.
    • Skin reactions can recur 1–4 weeks later (immune-mediated).
    • Avoid future re-exposure if known anaphylactic risk.

⚕️ ATLS 11th — Marine Trauma

ATLS
  • Shark and large predator attacks → primary cause of mortality is hemorrhage from extremity arterial injury → tourniquet on land + rapid transport.
  • Damage control: control hemorrhage first; complete primary survey; expedite resuscitation with balanced blood product ratios.
  • Rhabdomyolysis from prolonged immersion or sea snake/jellyfish envenomation — IV fluids, monitor K+ and Mg2+; avoid succinylcholine.
  • Compartment syndrome can occur after severe envenomation (stonefish, sea urchin) — measure pressures.
  • Wound contamination: empiric antibiotics covering Vibrio + Aeromonas + skin flora; consider hyperbaric oxygen for necrotizing wounds.
  • Spine injury: maintain c-spine precautions for diving accidents until cleared.

📗 Rosen's EM 10th — Marine Envenomation

Rosen's Ch.55 (Marine Envenomations)
  • Same overall framework — emphasis on hot-water immersion as universal first treatment for stingray, scorpaenid (lionfish/stonefish), sea urchin envenomation.
  • Pressure-immobilization — appropriate for sea snake, blue-ringed octopus, cone snail; contraindicated for box jellyfish (causes more nematocyst firing).
  • Vinegar use — Rosen's notes species-specificity: do use for box jellyfish (Chironex), controversial/avoid for Portuguese man-of-war (some studies show triggering) — when in doubt, use hot water.
  • Vibrio vulnificus — Rosen's emphasizes early empirical doxycycline + 3rd-generation cephalosporin in cirrhotic patients with saltwater exposure or oyster ingestion + skin findings.
  • Stonefish antivenom available in Australia (CSL); reserved for severe systemic envenomation.
  • Irukandji syndrome — magnesium sulfate (10 mg/kg) controls catecholamine surge; opioid for pain; phentolamine for refractory HTN.

End MCQ 1. First-line treatment for ALL marine envenomations (stingray, scorpaenid, sea urchin) is:
A. Cold pack
B. Hot-water immersion 110–114°F (43–46°C) for 30–90 min
C. Antivenom always
D. NSAIDs alone
Answer: B. Heat denatures heat-labile venom proteins. Test on uninjured limb first to avoid scald.
End MCQ 2. Empiric antibiotics for a saltwater wound in a cirrhotic patient should cover:
A. Vibrio + skin flora — doxycycline + ceftriaxone
B. Aeromonas only — ciprofloxacin
C. Strep only — penicillin
D. No antibiotics
Answer: A. Cirrhotic + saltwater = Vibrio risk. Doxycycline + 3rd-gen cephalosporin standard. Reference: Tintinalli p.1363.
End MCQ 3. The most venomous marine animal in the world is:
A. Blue-ringed octopus
B. Stonefish
C. Box jellyfish (Chironex fleckeri)
D. Sea snake
Answer: C. Chironex is most lethal — cardiotoxic + neurotoxic; can kill in minutes. Reference: Tintinalli p.1367.
End MCQ 4. Vinegar (5% acetic acid) is recommended for nematocyst inactivation in:
A. All jellyfish stings
B. Box jellyfish (Chironex)
C. Sea urchin
D. Stingray
Answer: B. Vinegar specifically inactivates Chironex nematocysts; species-dependent for others. Reference: Tintinalli p.1367.
End MCQ 5. Pressure-immobilization is APPROPRIATE first aid for:
A. Box jellyfish
B. Sea snake or blue-ringed octopus envenomation
C. All marine envenomations
D. Stingray
Answer: B. Pressure-immobilization for systemic neurotoxic envenomation (sea snake, blue-ringed octopus, cone snail). CONTRAINDICATED in box jellyfish.
End MCQ 6. Blue-ringed octopus venom acts via:
A. α-latrotoxin
B. Tetrodotoxin (Na+ channel blocker)
C. Hemolysis
D. Direct cardiotoxicity
Answer: B. Tetrodotoxin → flaccid paralysis. NO antidote — supportive ventilation until venom wears off (4–10 h).
End MCQ 7. Irukandji syndrome (Carukia barnesi) is BEST treated with:
A. Vinegar + magnesium sulfate IV + analgesia + antihypertensives
B. Antivenom only
C. Aggressive surgery
D. Cold packs
Answer: A. Vinegar to inactivate any remaining nematocysts; magnesium sulfate for catecholamine storm; opioids; phentolamine for HTN. Reference: Tintinalli p.1367.
End MCQ 8. Sea snake envenomation differs from terrestrial elapid bites in that:
A. Sea snake bites cause severe local pain immediately
B. Sea snake bites are often painless with delayed neurotoxicity + rhabdomyolysis
C. Antivenom is contraindicated
D. They are non-toxic
Answer: B. Sea snake bites painless + delayed neuro/myo features; rhabdomyolysis common. Polyvalent CSL antivenom + supportive ventilation.
End MCQ 9. Cone snail (Conus geographus) envenomation mortality is approximately:
A. 5%
B. 25%
C. 65%
D. 95%
Answer: C. C. geographus envenomation has ~65% mortality without aggressive supportive care.
End MCQ 10. The recommended antibiotic for a freshwater puncture wound is:
A. Vancomycin only
B. Fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin/levofloxacin) + first-gen cephalosporin
C. Doxycycline only
D. Penicillin
Answer: B. Aeromonas is the freshwater concern → fluoroquinolone. Add first-gen cephalosporin for skin flora.
End MCQ 11. Stonefish antivenom should be administered for:
A. All stonefish stings
B. Severe systemic envenomation only
C. Mild local pain
D. Never
Answer: B. Reserved for severe systemic envenomation; equine source — pretreat with antihistamines.
End MCQ 12. The marine wound infection most associated with cirrhotic patients is:
A. Strep pyogenes
B. Vibrio vulnificus (sepsis with hemorrhagic bullae)
C. Aeromonas hydrophila
D. Mycobacterium marinum
Answer: B. V. vulnificus in cirrhotic patients can cause fulminant sepsis with up to 50% mortality.
End MCQ 13. Mycobacterium marinum infection ('fish tank granuloma') is characterized by:
A. Acute fulminant sepsis
B. Indolent, chronic granuloma
C. Acute necrotizing fasciitis
D. Hemorrhagic bullae
Answer: B. M. marinum is indolent — chronic verrucous nodules along lymphatic distribution; treated with rifampin + ethambutol or clarithromycin.
End MCQ 14. Which is INAPPROPRIATE for general jellyfish sting management?
A. Salt water rinse
B. Hot-water immersion at 113°F (45°C) for 20 min
C. Fresh water rinse
D. Topical lidocaine
Answer: C. Fresh water triggers more nematocysts to fire — never use. Salt water rinse + hot water are best.
End MCQ 15. Tetrodotoxin is found in all of the following EXCEPT:
A. Pufferfish (Fugu)
B. Blue-ringed octopus
C. Cone snail
D. Certain newts
Answer: C. Cone snails contain conotoxins (Na+/Ca++ channel blockers), not tetrodotoxin. Pufferfish, blue-ringed octopus, and some newts have tetrodotoxin.
End MCQ 16. The cardiac complication of box jellyfish envenomation is best treated with:
A. Aspirin alone
B. CPR + box jellyfish antivenom + magnesium sulfate + supportive care
C. Cold packs only
D. Antibiotics
Answer: B. Cardiac arrest from Chironex requires immediate CPR, antivenom (CSL Australia), magnesium sulfate adjunct, ACLS support.
End MCQ 17. Crown-of-thorns starfish (Acanthaster planci) envenomation is best treated initially with:
A. Cold pack
B. Hot-water immersion + foreign body removal + analgesia
C. Antibiotics only
D. Vinegar
Answer: B. Hot-water immersion (110–114°F) for pain + remove visible spines + analgesia.
End MCQ 18. Which marine pathogen is associated with raw oyster ingestion in cirrhotic patients?
A. Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae
B. Vibrio vulnificus
C. Aeromonas hydrophila
D. Mycobacterium marinum
Answer: B. V. vulnificus from raw oysters can cause fulminant sepsis in cirrhotic patients — high mortality.
End MCQ 19. After a stonefish puncture wound, the main reason for hot-water immersion is:
A. To kill bacteria
B. To denature heat-labile venom proteins
C. To increase blood flow
D. To reduce edema
Answer: B. Most marine venoms are heat-labile proteins — heat denatures them, providing pain relief and inactivation.
End MCQ 20. A patient stung by Portuguese man-of-war should be treated with:
A. Vinegar (definitely)
B. Hot-water immersion + remove tentacles with gloved hand
C. Fresh water rinse
D. Aggressive scrubbing
Answer: B. For Portuguese man-of-war: hot water is reliable; vinegar is controversial (may trigger more firing in some species). Remove tentacles with gloves.

🔑 Key Points (High-Yield)

  1. Hot-water immersion 110–114°F is universal first-aid for most marine envenomations (denatures heat-labile venom proteins).
  2. Vinegar for box jellyfish (Chironex); avoid for Portuguese man-of-war (controversial — may trigger nematocysts).
  3. NEVER fresh water rinse for jellyfish — triggers nematocyst firing.
  4. Pressure-immobilization for sea snake, blue-ringed octopus, cone snail; NOT for box jellyfish.
  5. Tetrodotoxin (blue-ringed octopus, pufferfish): no antidote — supportive ventilation 4–10 h.
  6. Box jellyfish (Chironex) — most venomous marine animal; treat with vinegar + antivenom + Mg sulfate + ACLS.
  7. Irukandji syndrome: delayed catecholamine storm + HTN + "impending doom" → magnesium sulfate IV.
  8. Sea snake: painless bite + delayed neurotoxicity + rhabdomyolysis → polyvalent antivenom + supportive ventilation.
  9. Marine wound infection patterns differ:
    • Saltwater → Vibrio (especially in cirrhotic patients) → doxycycline + ceftriaxone
    • Freshwater → Aeromonas → fluoroquinolone
  10. Vibrio vulnificus in cirrhotic patient: 50% mortality even with treatment; raw oyster = high risk.
  11. Stonefish = most venomous fish; antivenom for severe systemic envenomation (CSL Australia).
  12. Stingray: shuffle-walk in shallow water; tail spine retains venom-loaded sheath.
  13. Coral wounds, sea urchin spines: remove foreign bodies; chronic granuloma if retained.
  14. Tetanus prophylaxis for all marine wounds.
  15. Mycobacterium marinum ("fish tank granuloma"): chronic indolent — rifampin + ethambutol or clarithromycin.
